title: Fly stitch
subtitle: A V-shaped open loop anchored by a straight stitch
excerpt: Fly stitch makes a V-shaped open loop with a straight anchoring stitch at the base, and one of the most versatile single stitches for scatter fills, leaf veins, and border lines.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886). Caulfeild and Saward, Dictionary of Needlework (1882), fly stitch entry.
heroPrompt: Row of fly stitches forming a decorative border on cream cotton, regular V shapes with short tails, close-up, natural light.

content.text: Fly stitch begins like a wide chain loop: bring the thread up at the left of the V, insert the needle to the right at the same level, and bring it up at the centre below. The thread sits under the needle tip to form the V. One anchor stitch at the centre holds it down.
Bring the needle up at A (left arm of the V).
Insert the needle at B (right arm of the V), level with A, and bring it up at C (the base point), keeping the thread under the needle.
Pull through until the V lies flat. Make one straight anchor stitch down from C to D. The length of CD sets the tail length.

items.symptom: The V arms are unequal lengths
items.cause: Points A and B are not level.
items.fix: Mark A and B with a light dot from a water-soluble pen before stitching.

items.symptom: The stitch looks squat rather than open
items.cause: Width between A and B is too narrow.
items.fix: Space A and B at least 6 mm apart for a clear V shape.

content.text: Fly stitch worked in columns makes leaf veins and feather fills. Placed individually it scatters well across backgrounds. Worked in rows with longer tails it becomes a border stitch.
